::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Audience.** System administrators, DevOps engineers, and on-call responders who maintain the
Ubuntu server that runs the Disaster Risk Management Information System (DRMIS / VBoS MIS) for
the National Disaster Management Office (NDMO), Vanuatu.

**Scope.** Hardware (Dell PowerEdge R750), firmware and out-of-band management (iDRAC9),
operating system (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS), storage and network fabric, the application stack that
runs on top (Docker Compose, Django, PostgreSQL / PostGIS, nginx, TiTiler), and the formal
**handover procedure from VBoS to NDMO** (see §14).

**Ownership note.** The server is currently hosted and operated by the **Vanuatu Bureau of
Statistics (VBoS)** on behalf of NDMO. Everywhere this document says *"the current
administrator"* it means VBoS (or the VBoS-designated sysadmin). Formal ownership and all
operational credentials transfer to NDMO at the sign-off recorded in §14.9.

**Companion documents.**
[`OVERVIEW.md`](../OVERVIEW.md) — application architecture ·
[`DEPLOYMENT_VM.md`](DEPLOYMENT_VM.md) — deploy runbook ·
[`DEPLOYMENT_MANUAL.md`](DEPLOYMENT_MANUAL.md) — non-Docker fallback ·
[`DEPLOYMENT_ROUTING.md`](DEPLOYMENT_ROUTING.md) — nginx routing ·
[`TITILER_SETUP.md`](TITILER_SETUP.md) — tile server internals.

**Document status.** Values marked **`TO BE VERIFIED`** require a server administrator with
physical / root access or an iDRAC login to confirm. The exact command to retrieve each value is
provided inline. Contact placeholders marked **`TO BE FILLED IN`** live in Appendix C and
must be completed at sign-off (§14.9 row 20).

**How to render this document.** The source is Quarto Markdown (`.qmd`). To produce a
self-contained HTML copy for sharing:

```bash
# Quarto must be installed on the renderer's workstation, not on the server.
# https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/
quarto render docs/DMIS_HOST.qmd --to html
# → docs/DMIS_HOST.html  (single-file, embedded CSS/fonts, ready to email)
```

Do **not** render on a machine with the GitHub remote configured *while §14.7 still holds
plaintext credentials* (the `.gitignore` guard blocks accidental `git add` of the `.qmd`
and of the rendered `.html`, but be careful with `rsync`, email attachments, or copying to
cloud storage). See §14.7 handling policy (Option B).
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Ownership status at time of writing.**

There is one logical network — the **Vanuatu Government (GoV) private WAN / intranet
(`vangov.local`)**. VBoS and NDMO both sit on it, in different IP segments and different
buildings.

| Dimension | Today | After handover |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical location** | **VBoS office, Port Vila** — VBoS server room, VBoS A/B power feeds, VBoS-owned rack + switch port | **NDMO facility** — NDMO rack, NDMO power, NDMO switch port (new building) |
| **Logical network** | Vanuatu Government private network (`vangov.local`) | Vanuatu Government private network (`vangov.local`) — **unchanged** |
| **IP allocation** | **VBoS segment** — host `10.4.26.55/24`, iDRAC `10.4.26.51/24` (DHCP), gateway `10.4.26.1` | **NDMO segment** — new NDMO-issued subnet, new gateway |
| **DNS (authoritative)** | `10.255.134.24`, `10.255.134.5` (GoV/ministry resolvers) — unchanged | `10.255.134.24`, `10.255.134.5` — unchanged |
| **Credentials** | Held by **VBoS (current administrator)** — `ndmoadmin` + iDRAC `root` (§14.7) | Rotated and reissued to NDMO sysadmins (§14.7.1) |

- Host OS login today: `ssh ndmoadmin@10.4.26.55` (SSH key-based, password auth disabled).
- iDRAC9 login today: `https://10.4.26.51/` — built-in `root` account.

**Practical consequence: NDMO can already reach the server today** (subject to GoV WAN ACLs)
from NDMO seats on the same GoV network — SSH on `10.4.26.55`, iDRAC at `10.4.26.51`, and
Cockpit at `https://10.4.26.55:9090/` should all resolve from NDMO before any physical move.
This makes **pre-handover dry-runs** possible and encouraged (§14.3 step "NDMO dry-run").

**Planned handover — Option 1 (confirmed).** The server will **physically move** to an NDMO
facility (new rack, new switch port) and receive a **new NDMO-segment IP** on the same GoV
WAN. Because the source and destination networks are one shared GoV network, the cutover is
not a cross-network migration — it's a **clean subnet reassignment within the GoV WAN**:

1. **Pre-allocate the new NDMO static IP** in a netplan drop-in **before** the move (host +
   iDRAC), validated with a dry-run from NDMO over the GoV WAN.
2. **Power down, relocate, recable, power up.** On boot at the NDMO rack, netplan applies
   the new static IP in one step — **no DHCP detour** needed.
3. **Update application config** (`ALLOWED_HOSTS`, `DJANGO_VM_HOST`, nginx `server_name`,
   frontend `VITE_API_HOST`) and **rotate all credentials** (§14.7.1).

The DHCP-fallback route is documented in §14.4 in case the pre-allocation path is blocked.
The full step-by-step procedure is in **§14 — Handover to NDMO**.
:::

# 2. Physical hardware — Dell PowerEdge R750

## 2.1 Chassis & platform

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| Manufacturer | Dell Inc. |
| Model | PowerEdge R750 |
| Family | PowerEdge |
| SKU | `SKU=090E;ModelName=PowerEdge R750` |
| Service tag (Dell ID) | **`BCLLJ54`** — also printed on the pull-out information card on the front bezel (Figure 2.1.1) |
| Express Service Code | `24706476328` |
| Chassis serial | `BCLLJ54` (matches service tag) |
| System board | Dell `0K8F35`, baseboard serial `.BCLLJ54.CNFCP0047H00KB.` |
| Chassis type | 23 — Rack Mount Chassis (2U) |
| BIOS vendor | Dell Inc. |
| BIOS version | **1.14.1** |
| BIOS date | 2024-03-11 |
| Firmware age | ~2 years at time of writing — quarterly firmware review recommended (§13) |
| TPM | Nuvoton NPCT75x TPM 2.0, firmware 7.2.3.1 |

Retrieve live:

```bash
# Most values are exposed in DMI/SMBIOS (no root required)
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/sys_vendor          # Manufacturer
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/product_name        # Model
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/product_family      # Family
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/product_sku         # SKU (includes model string)
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/board_name          # System board part number
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/chassis_type        # Chassis type code
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/bios_vendor         # BIOS vendor
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/bios_version        # BIOS version
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/bios_date           # BIOS date

# Serials require root via dmidecode
sudo dmidecode -s system-serial-number    # Service tag
sudo dmidecode -s baseboard-serial-number # Baseboard serial
sudo dmidecode -t chassis                 # Chassis detail
sudo dmidecode -t bios                    # BIOS detail incl. characteristics

# Platform overview + firmware age (relative to install date)
hostnamectl
fwupdmgr get-devices                      # TPM + other firmware-managed devices
```

## 2.2 CPU

Two sockets populated with identical processors:

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| Model | **Intel® Xeon® Silver 4309Y** (3rd Gen "Ice Lake-SP") |
| Sockets populated | 2 of 2 |
| Cores per socket | 8 |
| Threads per core | 2 (Hyper-Threading enabled) |
| **Total logical CPUs** | **32** |
| Base frequency | 2.80 GHz |
| Max turbo frequency | 3.60 GHz |
| Min frequency (idle) | 0.80 GHz |
| Cache | L1d 768 KiB (16×), L1i 512 KiB (16×), L2 20 MiB (16×), **L3 24 MiB (12 MiB per socket)** |
| Instruction set | AVX-512 (incl. VNNI, VBMI, BITALG), SHA-NI, AES-NI, VT-x, VT-d |
| NUMA topology | 2 nodes — node 0: even CPUs (0,2,…,30), 15.5 GB; node 1: odd CPUs (1,3,…,31), 16.1 GB |

Retrieve live:

```bash
lscpu
numactl --hardware
cat /proc/cpuinfo | head -30
```

## 2.3 Memory (RAM)

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| Installed capacity (visible to OS) | **32,347,572 kB ≈ 30.85 GiB** usable |
| Hardware capacity (nominal) | **32 GiB** (2 × 16 GB DDR4 RDIMM) |
| DIMM slots populated | **2 of 32** — slot **A1** (CPU 0, channel A) and **B1** (CPU 1, channel A) |
| DIMM part number | **Micron `18ASF2G72PDZ-3G2R1`** (16 GB 2Rx8 DDR4-3200 RDIMM, JEDEC vendor `0x002C`) |
| DIMM rated speed | **3200 MT/s** (PC4-25600) |
| DIMM running speed | **2666 MT/s** — the Xeon Silver 4309Y's memory controller tops out at 2666; DIMMs are down-clocked accordingly (this is expected, not a fault) |
| DIMM voltage | 1.2 V |
| DIMM rank / form factor | 2 ranks · RDIMM (registered + ECC) |
| DIMM serial numbers | A1 = `398DFD28` · B1 = `398E16E0` |
| NUMA distribution | node 0: 15,469 MB · node 1: 16,120 MB |
| Swap | 8 GiB |
| Max supported | **32 DIMM slots total** (16 per CPU, 8 channels × 2 DIMMs/ch); platform ceiling per SMBIOS memory-array entry = **12 TB** |
| ECC | Yes (multi-bit ECC, standard for RDIMM) |

::: {.callout-important}
**Memory is heavily under-populated.** Only 2 of 32 slots are filled, and the two DIMMs sit on
**one channel per CPU** — this means the server is running in **single-channel mode per
socket**, not the 8-channel mode the Ice Lake platform supports. Expected consequence: memory
bandwidth is a small fraction of nameplate. Not a correctness issue, but worth documenting so
future capacity planning (Redis, Celery workers, a larger PostGIS dataset, or heavier TiTiler
workloads) includes a DIMM population upgrade for proper multi-channel balance.
:::

Live DIMM inventory:

```bash
sudo dmidecode -t 16        # Physical memory array capabilities
sudo dmidecode -t 17        # Every DIMM slot (populated + empty)
sudo dmidecode -t 17 | grep -E "Locator|Size|Speed|Part Number|Manufacturer|Serial"
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Capacity planning.** The live application currently uses ~3 GiB with 12 GiB of buffer/cache
and 27 GiB available. There is plenty of headroom in the short term; before adding Redis +
Celery + heavier TiTiler concurrency (see §13), either raise RAM by populating the remaining
DIMM slots (ideally 8 matched DIMMs per CPU for full-channel operation) or budget for an
additional worker host.
:::

## 2.4 Storage subsystem

The server has **two independent storage controllers** by design:

1. **Dell BOSS-S2** (Boot Optimized Storage Solution) — a mirrored pair of M.2 SATA SSDs on a
   Marvell `88SE9230` PCIe card. Hosts the Ubuntu operating system only.
2. **Dell PERC H755** (Broadcom/LSI MegaRAID `SAS39xx`) — the main front-bay RAID controller.
   Presents one large virtual disk used for bulk data (`/mnt/ndmo_share`).

| Device | Size | Type | Controller | Role | Mount |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sdb` | 447.1 GiB | SATA (BOSS M.2 mirror) | BOSS-S2 (`88SE9230`) | OS boot | `/boot/efi`, `/boot`, `/` |
| `sda` | 65.5 TiB | SAS (HW RAID virtual disk) | PERC H755 | Bulk / share | `/mnt/ndmo_share` |

Partition & LVM layout on the boot device (`sdb`):

```
sdb
├─ sdb1   1 GiB   EFI System Partition   → /boot/efi
├─ sdb2   2 GiB   ext4 boot              → /boot
└─ sdb3 444 GiB   LVM PV (VG "ubuntu-vg")
         └─ ubuntu-lv  100 GiB  ext4     → /
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Only 100 GiB of the 444 GiB LVM physical volume is currently allocated to the root LV.
Roughly **344 GiB of free VG space** remains — you can extend `/` on demand with
`sudo lvextend -L +XG /dev/ubuntu-vg/ubuntu-lv && sudo resize2fs /dev/ubuntu-vg/ubuntu-lv`.
:::

Data device (`sda`, PERC H755) — **real configuration, pulled live from the iDRAC**:

```
PERC H755 Adapter (PCI Slot 2)
├─ Firmware:          52.26.0-5179
├─ Onboard cache:     8192 MB
├─ Encryption:        Capable, mode = None (drives not encrypted at rest)
├─ Patrol Read:       Automatic
├─ Copyback:          ON
├─ PersistHotspare:   Disabled  ◀── no dedicated hot spare
│
└─ Virtual Disk 239  —  Layout: RAID-5  ·  67,063 GB  ·  State: Online
   ├─ Read policy:    Read-Ahead
   ├─ Write policy:   Write-Back
   ├─ Stripe size:    256 KB
   ├─ Media:          HDD, SAS
   └─ Remaining redundancy: 1  (can survive exactly one drive failure)

Physical disks (10 × Toshiba SAS 8 TB HDD, all Online, no predictive failures):
  Bay 0:  7451.5 GB  TOSHIBA  SN 9470A0JXFGAH
  Bay 1:  7451.5 GB  TOSHIBA  SN 9460A0RYFGAH
  Bay 2:  7451.5 GB  TOSHIBA  SN 9470A0K1FGAH
  Bay 3:  7451.5 GB  TOSHIBA  SN 9470A0H9FGAH
  Bay 4:  7451.5 GB  TOSHIBA  SN 9470A0N9FGAH
  Bay 5:  7451.5 GB  TOSHIBA  SN 9470A0GRFGAH
  Bay 6:  7451.5 GB  TOSHIBA  SN 9470A0K9FGAH
  Bay 7–9: Toshiba SAS 8 TB (same spec)

vg_data  65.49 TiB total  |  10.00 TiB allocated  |  55.49 TiB FREE
└─ lv_samba  10 TiB  ext4  → /mnt/ndmo_share
              └─ df -h:  Size 10T  ·  Used 28K  ·  Avail 9.5T  ·  Use% 1%
                         (the ~500 GiB delta is ext4 metadata + 5 % root-reserved blocks)
```

Of the 65.5 TiB virtual disk, only **10 TiB is currently allocated** to the Samba share
(`lv_samba`). **The remaining ~55.5 TiB is not spare — it is the target for DRMIS data
growth**: large raster files (Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs served by TiTiler), GeoJSON / vector
layers, PMTiles caches, the PostgreSQL/PostGIS data directory, and on-box backups.

::: {.callout-important}
**Finding — DRMIS data currently lives on the OS disk, not on the PERC volume.**

Live check at time of writing:

```bash
$ du -sh vbos-backend/raster_data/ && df -h vbos-backend/raster_data/
8.0K   vbos-backend/raster_data/
Filesystem                         Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-ubuntu--lv   98G   21G   73G  22% /     ← 100 GiB OS LV

$ docker volume inspect vm_postgres_data | grep Mountpoint
"Mountpoint": "/var/lib/docker/volumes/vm_postgres_data/_data"       ← also on the OS LV
```

Both the raster store (`vbos-backend/raster_data/`) and the Docker volume holding PostgreSQL
/ PostGIS data are on the **100 GiB root logical volume** on the BOSS-S2 mirror. That disk
can only hold a handful of real-world COGs before `/` fills. The 55.5 TiB of PERC capacity
below is where this data is supposed to land; today it is effectively unused. Migrate
before DRMIS ingests significant production data — see the proposed layout below and §13
checklist row *"DRMIS data relocation"*.
:::

### Proposed DRMIS data layout on `vg_data` (≈55 TiB reserved)

This is a **proposal** — confirm sizes with the DRMIS dev team at handover and adjust to the
expected data footprint. All LVs are `ext4`, created from `vg_data`, and can be grown online
with `lvextend` + `resize2fs`.

| Logical volume | Initial size | Mount point | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lv_samba` (existing) | 10 TiB | `/mnt/ndmo_share` | End-user Samba share (`NDMO-DRMIS-Share`, §7.2) |
| `lv_rasters` | 15 TiB | `/srv/drmis/rasters` | Source + processed COGs for TiTiler (`vbos-backend/raster_data/` bind-mounted here) |
| `lv_vectors` | 2 TiB | `/srv/drmis/vectors` | GeoJSON, Shapefile, FlatGeobuf, PMTiles vector tiles |
| `lv_postgres` | 5 TiB | `/var/lib/drmis-postgres` | Bind-mounted into `vm-postgres-1` in place of the named Docker volume |
| `lv_backups` | 5 TiB | `/srv/drmis/backups` | Nightly `pg_dump`, media tarballs, docker image snapshots (today stored in `/mnt/ndmo_share/backups/drmis` — see §9.2) |
| **Allocated total** | **37 TiB** | — | — |
| **Free for future growth** | **≈28 TiB** | — | Grow any of the above with `lvextend` on demand |

Rough creation sequence (to run at the migration window, not now):

```bash
# 1. Create the new LVs from free extents in vg_data
sudo lvcreate -L 15T -n lv_rasters  vg_data
sudo lvcreate -L  2T -n lv_vectors  vg_data
sudo lvcreate -L  5T -n lv_postgres vg_data
sudo lvcreate -L  5T -n lv_backups  vg_data

# 2. Format and mount
for lv in rasters vectors postgres backups; do
  sudo mkfs.ext4 -L drmis-$lv /dev/vg_data/lv_$lv
  sudo mkdir -p /srv/drmis/$lv /var/lib/drmis-postgres
done
# Add matching entries to /etc/fstab (use LABEL=drmis-rasters etc. for portability)

# 3. Relocate raster_data  (stack must be stopped first — it's read-only anyway today)
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml stop vm-titiler vm-web
sudo rsync -aHAX vbos-backend/raster_data/ /srv/drmis/rasters/
sudo mv vbos-backend/raster_data vbos-backend/raster_data.old
sudo ln -s /srv/drmis/rasters vbos-backend/raster_data
# (or update the compose bind-mount source to /srv/drmis/rasters)

# 4. Relocate PostgreSQL data — destructive, do with a dump + restore
#    a. pg_dump from the current container into /srv/drmis/backups/pre-migrate.dump
#    b. Stop vm-postgres, remove the named volume vm_postgres_data
#    c. Change the compose file to bind-mount /var/lib/drmis-postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data
#    d. Start vm-postgres → it initialises a fresh cluster on the new volume
#    e. Restore the dump
```

Growing any LV later (online, no downtime, no unmount):

```bash
sudo lvextend -L +1T /dev/vg_data/lv_rasters
sudo resize2fs  /dev/vg_data/lv_rasters
```

Growing `lv_samba` (end-user share) uses the exact same pattern — see §6.

::: {.callout-important}
**Critical finding — RAID-5 on 10 × 8 TB HDDs with no persistent hot spare.** This array
tolerates exactly **one** drive failure. If a second drive fails **during** the rebuild (which
on 8 TB SAS HDDs is typically 24-72 hours depending on load), the entire 10 TiB of data in
`/mnt/ndmo_share` is lost. Because:

- the rebuild window is long (slow spinning disks + 30% rebuild rate),
- there is **no dedicated hot spare** (`PersistHotspare = Disabled`), so the operator must be
  paged in to physically replace a failed drive before the rebuild can even start,
- and the drives are all the same model / age / manufacturing lot (sequential serials), which
  elevates the probability of correlated failures,

two recommendations — pick at least one before production data grows further:

1. **Preferred: reshape to RAID-6** (survives 2 simultaneous failures). This is destructive
   and requires a rebuild from backup.
2. **Minimum: assign a dedicated hot spare** — leave 9 drives in RAID-5, designate 1 as a
   global hot spare. One-drive failure triggers automatic rebuild with no operator input.

Both options are captured in §13 (production-readiness checklist).
:::

```bash
racadm storage get controllers -o | grep -A2 PERC
racadm storage get vdisks -o
racadm storage get pdisks -o
```

Retrieve live:

```bash
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,ROTA,TRAN
sudo pvs && sudo vgs && sudo lvs
sudo parted -l
df -hT
```

# 3. Out-of-band management — iDRAC9

## 3.1 What iDRAC is, and why it matters

The **integrated Dell Remote Access Controller (iDRAC9)** is a baseboard management controller
(BMC) built into every R750. It is a small, independent computer running its own operating
system on a dedicated ARM SoC, with its own network interface and its own power rail. It stays
up and reachable **even when the main server is powered off**, as long as the PSUs are plugged
in.

From iDRAC you can:

- Power the server on/off/cycle remotely (equivalent to walking to the server and pressing the button);
- See the physical BIOS/UEFI boot screen and type at the console via the **Virtual Console (HTML5 KVM)**;
- Mount an ISO from your laptop as if it were a DVD in the drive (**Virtual Media**), e.g. to reinstall Ubuntu without a crash cart;
- Read hardware health (CPU temp, DIMM status, PSU draw, fan RPM, NIC link state, RAID health);
- Update BIOS, iDRAC firmware, NIC firmware, and PERC firmware from `.d9` bundles;
- Read and clear the System Event Log (SEL) and the Lifecycle Log;
- Get email / SNMP / Redfish alerts for hardware faults.

::: {.callout-important}
iDRAC is the single most important tool for an on-call responder. If the host is unreachable
over SSH, iDRAC is almost certainly how you will recover it.
:::

### First-time setup / recovery checklist

If you have physical access to the front of the server:

1. Press the **System ID** button on the front bezel to locate this server in the rack (the blue LED on the rear will blink).
2. Attach a crash cart (VGA + USB keyboard) or use the iDRAC front USB port.
3. At POST, press **F2** → iDRAC Settings → **Network** to view/set the iDRAC IP.
4. Set:
   - Enable NIC: **Yes**
   - NIC Selection: **Dedicated**
   - IPv4 → Static: `<assigned-iDRAC-IP> / mask / gateway`
   - DNS server: ministry DNS (currently `10.255.134.24`, `10.255.134.5` via DHCP — these are the Vanuatu Government internal resolvers and should be hard-coded when going static)
5. Exit and apply; the server will continue booting Ubuntu while iDRAC re-announces on the new address.
6. Browse to `https://<iDRAC-IP>/`, log in with the rotated `root` password, and immediately:
   - Create at least **one additional named admin user** per operator (`iDRAC Settings → Users`) with a strong password and 2FA where supported;
   - Confirm IPMI over LAN is disabled (currently Disabled — good);
   - Configure NTP pointing to a local time source (Vanuatu: `pool.ntp.org` or a ministry NTP host);
   - Configure email alerts (SMTP host + recipient);
   - Upload a CA-signed TLS certificate (self-signed warning otherwise).

## 3.5 Hardware health monitoring

From the iDRAC UI (`Dashboard` and `System → Overview`):

- **System Health** summary — single green / amber / red indicator
- **Batteries** — CMOS coin cell state
- **Cooling** — per-fan RPM and threshold
- **CPUs** — model, frequency, throttling events, thermal margin
- **Intrusion** — chassis intrusion sensor
- **Memory** — DIMM population map, size, speed, manufacturer, SBE / DBE history
- **Power Supplies** — wattage draw per PSU, input voltage, redundancy state
- **Temperatures** — inlet, exhaust, per-CPU
- **Voltages** — all monitored rails
- **Removable Flash Media** — BOSS card status, internal SD card (if any)
- **Storage** — PERC H755 controller, virtual disks, physical disks, SMART predictive alerts

From the CLI (`racadm` — run on the host OS after install):

```bash
racadm gethwinventory         # Exhaustive HW inventory (CPU, DIMM, PSU, storage, NICs)
racadm getsel                 # System event log
racadm getsensorinfo          # Live sensor readings (temps, fans, voltages, power)
racadm storage get controllers
racadm storage get vdisks
racadm storage get pdisks
```

## 3.6 Virtual Console & Virtual Media

The Virtual Console is an HTML5 KVM viewer that gives you the physical monitor and keyboard
over the network. Use it to:

- Boot into BIOS / UEFI (press F2/F11 at POST);
- Run through the Ubuntu installer when reimaging;
- Troubleshoot boot failures (e.g. to see a kernel panic or an `initramfs>` prompt);
- Access GRUB rescue.

Virtual Media lets you map an ISO from your laptop; combined with the Virtual Console you can
reinstall Ubuntu from anywhere without a USB stick.

**Usage pattern:**

1. iDRAC UI → **Console** → **Launch Virtual Console** (HTML5).
2. In the console window → **Virtual Media** → **Connect Virtual Media** → map an ISO (e.g. `ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso`).
3. iDRAC UI → **Configuration → BIOS → One-time Boot** → set next boot to **Virtual CD/DVD/ISO**.
4. iDRAC UI → **Power → Reset (warm boot)**.

## 3.7 Firmware lifecycle (BIOS / iDRAC / PERC / NIC)

Dell bundles firmware as:

- Dell Update Packages (DUP) — `.BIN` files that run on Linux;
- `.d9` bundles for iDRAC Lifecycle Controller;
- Update Catalogue served by Dell (via iDRAC Lifecycle Controller online update).

Recommended cadence: check quarterly, apply at the next maintenance window.

Procedures:

- **Easy path (from iDRAC UI):** `Maintenance → System Update → Manual Update` → upload the DUP.
- **One-shot path (from Ubuntu via racadm):**

  ```bash
  racadm update -f /path/to/BIOS_...EXE   # Schedules update at next reboot
  racadm getupdatestatus
  ```

- **OS path for NIC / BOSS / PERC firmware:** download the Linux DUP from `dell.com/support` using the service tag, make executable, run as root.
- **Fwupd (only a subset of devices):** `sudo fwupdmgr refresh && sudo fwupdmgr update` — today this covers PERC H755, BCM57416 10 GbE, BCM5719, BCM5720, UEFI dbx, BOSS-S2 controller, TPM microcode, CPU microcode, and Matrox video BIOS (but **not** BIOS itself or iDRAC).

::: {.callout-tip}
After any BIOS / iDRAC / PERC firmware update, re-check DIMM population, NIC link state, and
RAID virtual disk health. Record the old and new firmware versions in your change log.
:::

## 3.8 The `racadm` CLI on this host

Dell does not publish an Ubuntu 24.04 build of `srvadmin-idracadm8`, and the closest supported
repo (`linux.dell.com/repo/community/openmanage/.../jammy`) is not reachable from the NDMO LAN.
Instead, `ndmo-drmis-01` has a **thin wrapper** at `/usr/local/bin/racadm` that forwards every
command to the iDRAC's own racadm over SSH. This has two operational benefits:

1. **No version skew** — each racadm call runs inside the iDRAC, so the CLI version always
   matches the firmware.
2. **No separate credentials on the host** — SSH keys or interactive passwords to the iDRAC
   are the only secret needed.

The wrapper reads its default target from `/etc/racadm.conf`:

```
host=10.4.26.51
user=root
```

Override per-invocation with `--host`, `--user`, or the `RACADM_HOST` / `RACADM_USER`
environment variables.

Usage is identical to a native racadm:

```bash
racadm getversion
racadm getsysinfo
racadm license view
racadm storage get vdisks -o
racadm getsel | tail -20
```

::: {.callout-tip}
**Make it passwordless.** The SSH prompt gets old quickly. Generate an Ed25519 key on the
host, then enrol the public key with iDRAC:

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f ~/.ssh/idrac_ed25519
# iDRAC UI → iDRAC Settings → Users → root → SSH Key Authentication → Paste public key,
# or CLI:
racadm sshpkauth -i 2 -k 1 -t 1 -f ~/.ssh/idrac_ed25519.pub
```

After that, `racadm ...` invocations run without any password prompt.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Alternative (if/when Dell's repo becomes reachable).** If the NDMO LAN is later allowed
outbound HTTPS to `linux.dell.com` and `dl.dell.com`, you can replace the wrapper with the
native CLI:

```bash
echo 'deb https://linux.dell.com/repo/community/openmanage/11000/jammy jammy main' | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/linux.dell.com.sources.list
wget -qO- https://linux.dell.com/repo/pgp_pubkeys/0x1285491434D8786F.asc | \
  sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/dell.gpg
sudo apt update
sudo apt install srvadmin-idracadm8
```

Then remove `/usr/local/bin/racadm` and `/etc/racadm.conf` — the `srvadmin-idracadm8` package
provides its own `racadm` at `/opt/dell/srvadmin/bin/idracadm7`.
:::

## 3.9 Baseline iDRAC hardening checklist

- [x] Factory password (`calvin`) changed — VBoS holds a rotated `root` password (§14.7)
- [ ] Local `root` disabled, or renamed + limited to emergency break-glass
- [ ] One named admin account per operator (no shared logins) — **currently only `root` exists**
- [ ] SSH key or cert auth preferred; password accounts use ≥16-char random passwords
- [x] IPMI over LAN **disabled** (confirmed via `racadm get iDRAC.IPMILan`)
- [ ] Telnet disabled (it ships disabled on iDRAC9; confirm with screenshot in Fig. 3.3.1)
- [ ] TLS certificate is CA-signed (not self-signed) — **currently self-signed**
- [ ] iDRAC reachable only from admin VLAN / jump host — **currently reachable from any host on the VBoS segment (`10.4.26.0/24`) of the GoV WAN, and potentially from the wider GoV network subject to WAN ACLs**
- [ ] NTP source matches the host (§4)
- [ ] Email alerts configured to the NDMO operations mailbox
- [ ] Redfish / SNMP access audited; remove unused community strings (SNMP community is still the default `public`)
- [ ] DNS auto-register enabled after NDMO AD DNS policy confirmed (currently **Disabled**)
- [ ] Convert iDRAC IPv4 from DHCP to **Static** once NDMO finalises the reservation (§14.5)
- [ ] Lockdown Mode considered for routine operations (this server is licenced **iDRAC9 Enterprise** — Lockdown Mode is a Datacenter-only feature, so not available here)

## 4.2 Package management

- Primary package source: `apt` with Ubuntu's official archive (noble / noble-updates / noble-security).
- Third-party sources currently active: **Docker CE** (`download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu noble stable`).
- **Recommended cadence:**
  - Weekly: `sudo apt update && sudo apt list --upgradable` to preview;
  - Monthly: schedule a maintenance window, `sudo apt upgrade -y`, then reboot if a new kernel arrived;
  - Leave `unattended-upgrades` on for security-only patches between windows.

## 4.3 Timezone & clock

`timedatectl` currently reports:

```
Time zone: Asia/Magadan (+11, +1100)
System clock synchronized: no
NTP service: active
```

Vanuatu is **UTC+11 year-round** and has the same offset as Magadan today, so clocks are
*visually* correct — but for auditability, logs, email timestamps, and any future integration
with Pacific services, this should be set to the canonical zone for Vanuatu:

```bash
sudo timedatectl set-timezone Pacific/Efate
```

The Django stack's Docker Compose already defaults to `Pacific/Fiji`; `Pacific/Efate` is the
correct Vanuatu zone and should be used consistently.

`System clock synchronized: no` means `timesyncd` has not yet synchronised since the last boot;
check with:

```bash
timedatectl timesync-status
systemctl status systemd-timesyncd
```

Consider pointing at a ministry-internal NTP source by editing `/etc/systemd/timesyncd.conf`
(`NTP=` line) and restarting.

## 4.4 SSH access policy

Current `sshd_config` (relevant lines):

```
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
AllowUsers ndmoadmin
```

This is correct and should be preserved:

- No direct root SSH;
- Password login disabled — **SSH keys only**;
- Only `ndmoadmin` may log in over SSH; additional admins must either (a) be added to
  `AllowUsers` after their public key is deployed, or (b) log in via iDRAC virtual console in
  break-glass scenarios.

SSH listens on TCP **22**. `fail2ban` is active and will ban IPs that brute-force.

To add a new admin:

```bash
sudo adduser --disabled-password <username>
sudo usermod -aG sudo,docker <username>
sudo mkdir -p /home/<username>/.ssh
sudo vim /home/<username>/.ssh/authorized_keys  # paste pubkey
sudo chown -R <username>:<username> /home/<username>/.ssh
sudo chmod 700 /home/<username>/.ssh
sudo chmod 600 /home/<username>/.ssh/authorized_keys
sudo sed -i 's/^AllowUsers ndmoadmin$/AllowUsers ndmoadmin <username>/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo systemctl reload ssh
```

## 4.5 Sudo / privilege

`ndmoadmin` is in the `sudo` group and the `docker` group. All privileged commands should be
invoked via `sudo`; do not share the `ndmoadmin` password or SSH key.

# 5. Storage layout

This is a logical restatement of §2.4, from the filesystem's point of view.

## 5.1 Mount points

**Current layout (today):**

| Mount | Device | Size | Purpose | Filesystem |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/` | `/dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-ubuntu--lv` | 98 GiB (22 % used) | OS root | ext4 |
| `/boot` | `sdb2` | 2 GiB | Kernel images, initramfs | ext4 |
| `/boot/efi` | `sdb1` | 1 GiB | EFI System Partition | vfat |
| `/mnt/ndmo_share` | `/dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_samba` | 10 TiB | Samba file share (see §7.2) | ext4 |
| `/var/lib/docker` | on `/` | grows on `/` | Docker images, volumes, containers | overlay2 |
| `/var/lib/docker/volumes/vm_postgres_data/_data` | on `/` | grows on `/` | **PostgreSQL data** for DRMIS — misplaced, see callout | — |
| `vbos-backend/raster_data/` | on `/` | grows on `/` | **DRMIS raster store** for TiTiler — misplaced, see callout | — |

::: {.callout-warning}
**Capacity risk — two data stores on the wrong disk.**

Both the PostgreSQL Docker volume **and** `vbos-backend/raster_data/` sit on the 100 GiB OS
LV (BOSS-S2 mirror). The VG holding `/` (`ubuntu-vg`, on `sdb3`) has only ~344 GiB of free
extents total, while the 55.5 TiB on `vg_data` (PERC H755) — which is where they are
*supposed* to live — sits unused. A handful of real COGs or a busy PostGIS workload will
push `/` past 85 % full very quickly. Relocate both stores to dedicated LVs on `vg_data` per
the proposed layout in **§2.4** — tracked in §13.
:::

**Target layout (after the §2.4 migration):**

| Mount | Device | Size | Purpose | Filesystem |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/mnt/ndmo_share` | `/dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_samba` | 10 TiB | Samba file share (unchanged) | ext4 |
| `/srv/drmis/rasters` | `/dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_rasters` | 15 TiB (grow on demand) | COGs / rasters served by TiTiler | ext4 |
| `/srv/drmis/vectors` | `/dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_vectors` | 2 TiB | GeoJSON / PMTiles / vector layers | ext4 |
| `/var/lib/drmis-postgres` | `/dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_postgres` | 5 TiB | PostgreSQL/PostGIS data dir (bind-mounted into `vm-postgres-1`) | ext4 |
| `/srv/drmis/backups` | `/dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_backups` | 5 TiB | Nightly `pg_dump`, media tarballs (replaces `/mnt/ndmo_share/backups/drmis/`) | ext4 |

The above totals 37 TiB, leaving ~28 TiB on `vg_data` free for future growth of any LV.

## 5.2 RAID health

Both RAID controllers are visible to iDRAC; the BOSS-S2 presents a hardware mirror to the OS
(no Linux `md` device). Preferred tooling order:

1. **`racadm`** (already installed as a wrapper — see §3.8) — works regardless of driver
   state and produces the same data the iDRAC UI shows;
2. **`perccli`** (optional native CLI) — Dell's MegaRAID tool, only needed for offline ops
   (pre-initialize a new VD, replace a drive, etc.).

```bash
# Via the racadm wrapper — no extra install required:
racadm storage get controllers -o              # Both controllers, full detail
racadm storage get vdisks -o                   # VDs: layout, size, state, stripe, cache
racadm storage get pdisks -o                   # PDs: model, size, state, SMART status
racadm getsel | grep -iE 'storage|disk|PERC|RAID' | tail -20

# If you install Dell's native perccli later (download from dell.com/support):
sudo perccli /c0 show all           # PERC H755 controller health
sudo perccli /c0/v0 show all        # Virtual disk 0
sudo perccli /c0/eall/sall show all # Physical disks
```

**Controller summary (retrieved live):**

| Controller | FQDD | Firmware | Cache | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PERC H755 Adapter (PCI Slot 2) | `RAID.Slot.2-1` | **52.26.0-5179** | 8192 MB | 10× 8 TB SAS HDD → **Virtual Disk 239** (RAID-5, 65.5 TiB) |
| BOSS-S2 (slimline slot 6) | `AHCI.SL.6-1` | — | none | 2× SATA M.2 SSD → **Virtual Disk 0** (RAID-1, 447 GiB, name `VD_R1_1`) |
| Onboard AHCI 1 / 2 | `AHCI.Embedded.*` | — | — | Unused |

Recommended schedule: patrol read weekly (iDRAC default is automatic), consistency check
monthly. Both are configurable via the iDRAC UI → **Storage → Controllers → PERC H755 →
Actions**.

## 5.3 Expansion plan

- **Grow `/`:** `sudo lvextend -L +50G /dev/ubuntu-vg/ubuntu-lv && sudo resize2fs /dev/ubuntu-vg/ubuntu-lv`
- **Grow `/mnt/ndmo_share`:** `sudo lvextend -L +1T /dev/vg_data/lv_samba && sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_samba`
- **Add more physical disks to PERC H755:** insert drives, then via iDRAC / perccli add to the existing RAID virtual disk or create a new one, then create a new PV / VG.

## 6.2 Published ports (listening on all interfaces)

| Port | Process / container | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 22/tcp | `sshd` | SSH |
| 80/tcp | `vm-nginx-1` (docker-proxy) | DRMIS web front door (serves SPA, proxies API / admin / TiTiler) |
| 111/tcp, 2049/tcp | `rpcbind`, NFS kernel server | Listening but **no exports** — see §7.3 |
| 139/tcp, 445/tcp | `smbd` | Samba share `NDMO-DRMIS-Share` — see §7.2 |
| 8000/tcp | `vm-web-1` (docker-proxy → gunicorn) | Django published directly for debugging — should be closed in firewall |
| 8002/tcp | `vm-titiler-1` (docker-proxy) | TiTiler — published so the frontend can hit it cross-origin |
| 9090/tcp | **`cockpit.socket`** (systemd-activated, owned by PID 1) | **Cockpit — host web console.** See §7.4 |
| 35683/tcp, 42509/tcp, 42939/tcp, 43467/tcp (loopback only) | `node` (Cursor / editor helpers running under `ndmoadmin`) | Local-only; safe to ignore |
| random high ports | `rpc.mountd`, `rpc.statd` (NFS helpers) | Part of the NFS daemon set — disable with NFS (§7.3) |

## 6.3 Host firewall (UFW) — **actual current state**

UFW is **active** with default policy `deny (incoming) / allow (outgoing) / deny (routed)` and
logging enabled (`low`). The current allow-list:

| Port / proto | Source | Purpose | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| 22/tcp | Anywhere (IPv4 + IPv6) | SSH | Should be tightened to `AllowUsers` + jump-host subnet after handover (see §12, §14.7) |
| 80/tcp | Anywhere (IPv4 + IPv6) | DRMIS web UI | OK for NDMO LAN; add a 443/tcp rule once TLS is in place (see §13) |
| 443/tcp | Anywhere (IPv4 + IPv6) | **TLS port is open in firewall but nothing listens on it yet** | Harmless (no listener) but confusing — leave the rule, add the listener |
| 139/tcp, 445/tcp | Anywhere (IPv4 + IPv6) | Samba | **Tighten to NDMO file-share subnets only** (§7.2 + §12) |
| 9090/tcp | Anywhere (IPv4 + IPv6) | **Cockpit** | **Tighten to admin subnet / VPN only** — Cockpit is a full privileged UI (§7.4) |

Docker publishes additional ports (`8000`, `8002`) via `iptables DOCKER` chain, which bypasses
UFW. These are reachable from the LAN whether or not UFW has a matching rule. To block them
without breaking the app, use `DOCKER-USER` chain rules or bind the published ports to
`127.0.0.1` in `docker-compose.yml`.

```bash
sudo ufw status verbose
sudo ufw status numbered
# Example tightening (adjust CIDRs for NDMO admin VLAN):
sudo ufw delete allow 9090/tcp
sudo ufw allow from 10.4.26.0/24 to any port 9090 proto tcp comment 'Cockpit (LAN only)'
```

## 7.1 Service management quick reference

```bash
systemctl status docker
sudo systemctl restart docker
sudo systemctl disable --now ModemManager wpa_supplicant   # Safe to remove on a wired server
journalctl -u docker -n 200 --no-pager
```

## 7.2 Samba (`NDMO-DRMIS-Share`)

Current `/etc/samba/smb.conf` (relevant stanza):

```ini
[NDMO-DRMIS-Share]
   path = /mnt/ndmo_share
   writable = yes
   guest ok = yes
   browsable = yes
```

::: {.callout-important}
**Critical finding.** The share is configured with `guest ok = yes` + `writable = yes` on a
**10 TiB** volume. Any user on the NDMO LAN can read, write, and delete files without
authentication. This should be replaced with user-authenticated access (`valid users =`,
`force user =`, `guest ok = no`) and/or firewalled to the specific subnets that need access.
:::

## 7.3 NFS

NFS daemons are running (`rpcbind`, `nfs-mountd`, `nfs-idmapd`, `rpc-statd`, `nfsdcld`,
`nfs-blkmap`, `fsidd`) but `/etc/exports` is empty. Recommendation: either disable the full NFS
stack or, at minimum, block ports 111 and 2049 in UFW until an actual export is configured:

```bash
sudo systemctl disable --now nfs-server nfs-idmapd nfs-blkmap rpc-statd rpcbind nfsdcld fsidd
```

## 7.4 Cockpit — host web console

The host runs **Cockpit**, a Red Hat-maintained browser UI for Linux server administration.
It is socket-activated by systemd and reachable at:

```
https://10.4.26.55:9090/
```

(TLS is self-signed by default; the browser will warn on first connect — accept the cert or
install a proper one — see §12.)

**Installed Cockpit modules on this host:**

| Package | What it adds to the UI |
|---|---|
| `cockpit`, `cockpit-bridge`, `cockpit-ws` | Core web service (socket-activated on `:9090`) |
| `cockpit-system` | Dashboard: CPU/RAM/disk graphs, hostname, time, kernel, logs |
| `cockpit-storaged` | Disks, partitions, LVM, NFS mounts, BTRFS (visual equivalent of `lsblk + pvs/vgs/lvs`) |
| `cockpit-networkmanager` | Network interfaces, IP, bonding, bridging, VLAN, DNS |
| `cockpit-packagekit` | Apt updates visible in-browser |
| `cockpit-file-sharing` | **The module used to create `/mnt/ndmo_share` as a Samba share** |

Cockpit authenticates using **regular OS accounts** — log in as `ndmoadmin` with the shell
password. If the account is in `sudo`, Cockpit exposes "Turn on administrative access" which
unlocks privileged panels.

```{=html}
<div class="screenshot-slot"><div class="screenshot-slot-inner"><strong>Figure 7.4.1 — Cockpit login and dashboard</strong><code>docs/screenshots/host/27-cockpit-dashboard.png</code><span class="hint">Open <code>https://10.4.26.55:9090/</code> in a browser (accept the self-signed cert), log in as <code>ndmoadmin</code>, click <em>Turn on administrative access</em>, and capture the default dashboard (Overview page) showing CPU, memory, disk usage, and hostname. Also capture the <em>File Sharing</em> page to show the <code>NDMO-DRMIS-Share</code> definition.</span><span class="annotate"><strong>Annotate:</strong> highlight the <em>Administrative access</em> toggle and the share listing.</span></div></div>
```

::: {.callout-important}
**Cockpit exposure review (security).** At present, UFW opens `9090/tcp` from **Anywhere**
(see §6.3). Cockpit is a full privileged UI — anyone who can reach the port and guess a local
password has root-equivalent access through the "administrative access" toggle. Before or
during handover (§14.7), restrict 9090 to a specific admin VLAN or VPN CIDR, install a proper
TLS certificate at `/etc/cockpit/ws-certs.d/`, and ensure every shell account with sudo has a
strong unique password and SSH-key-only login.
:::

**Useful Cockpit commands from the shell:**

```bash
systemctl status cockpit.socket           # Is the socket listener active?
systemctl restart cockpit.socket          # Bounce the UI without rebooting the box
ls /etc/cockpit/ws-certs.d/               # TLS cert location (drop a .cert and matching .key here)
sudo cockpit-bridge --version             # Cockpit core version
```

# 8. Application stack (Docker Compose)

## 8.1 Overview

The DRMIS app runs as a single Docker Compose project named **`vm`**, defined at
`/var/www/disaster-project-mis/deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml`. All runtime state lives in named
volumes managed by Docker.

**Currently running containers (as of writing):**

| Name | Image | Published ports | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vm-nginx-1` | `nginx:alpine` | `80/tcp` | Reverse proxy + serves React SPA |
| `vm-web-1` | `vm-web` (built locally from `vbos-backend/Dockerfile`) | `8000/tcp` | Django 5.2 + Gunicorn (DRF API, admin) |
| `vm-titiler-1` | `vm-titiler` (built locally from `vbos-backend/titiler-local`) | `8002/tcp` | COG / GeoTIFF tile server |
| `vm-postgres-1` | `postgis/postgis:17-3.5` | (internal only) | PostgreSQL 17 + PostGIS 3.5 |

**Named Docker volumes:**

- `vm_postgres_data` — PostgreSQL on-disk cluster (the database lives here)
- `vm_static_volume` — Django `collectstatic` output, mounted read-only into nginx

**Bind mounts:**

- `vbos-backend/media/` → `/app/media` in `vm-web-1` (user uploads, PMTiles)
- `vbos-backend/raster_data/` → `/data` in `vm-titiler-1` (source COGs)
- `vbos-frontend/dist/` → `/usr/share/nginx/html` in `vm-nginx-1` (built SPA)
- `deploy/vm/nginx.conf` → `/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf` in `vm-nginx-1`

**Compose includes:** the repo-root `docker-compose.yml` merely includes
`vbos-backend/docker-compose.yml`, which is the **developer** stack (adds Redis, Celery worker
+ beat, MailHog, MkDocs). On this host we do **not** run the dev stack — only
`deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml`.

## 8.2 Routing (nginx)

From `deploy/vm/nginx.conf` — what each URL path does:

| Path | Proxied to | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `/titiler/` | `http://titiler:8000/` | Matched with `^~` to prevent SPA hijack |
| `/api/` | `http://web:8000` | API — `proxy_buffering off` (PMTiles byte-range support) |
| `/admin/` | `http://web:8000` | Django admin — `/admin` redirects with 301 to `/admin/` |
| `/api-token-auth/` | `http://web:8000` | DRF token auth endpoint |
| `/static/` | `alias /static/` | Django static (served from the `vm_static_volume`) |
| `/media/` | `http://web:8000` | User uploads — proxied for consistency |
| `/` (everything else) | `try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html` | SPA fallback; `/index.html` is never cached |

## 8.3 Configuration

| File | What it contains | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| `vbos-backend/.env` | `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY`, Django settings overrides | Present on host, never commit |
| `vbos-backend/.env.example` | Commented template | Reference for variable names |
| `vbos-frontend/.env.production.local` | `VITE_API_HOST`, `VITE_TITILER_API` | Build-time only |
| `deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml` | The stack | Source of truth |
| `deploy/vm/nginx.conf` | Reverse-proxy routes | Source of truth |

Canonical environment variables set for the Django container (non-secret):

```yaml
DJANGO_CONFIGURATION: Vm
DJANGO_DEBUG: "false"
DJANGO_DB_URL: postgis://postgres:postgres@postgres:5432/vbos
DJANGO_VM_HOST: http://10.252.0.158   # overridden; actual host is 10.4.26.55
POSTGRES_HOST: postgres
POSTGRES_DB: vbos
POSTGRES_USER: postgres
POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres           # ⚠️ Compose default — see §13
TZ: Pacific/Fiji                      # ⚠️ Should be Pacific/Efate
PORT: "8000"
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**Drift warning.** `DJANGO_VM_HOST` in compose defaults to `http://10.252.0.158`; the actual
host IP is `10.4.26.55`. Confirm this does not affect absolute URL generation in Django
(`SITE_URL`, `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, CSRF trusted origins).
:::

## 8.4 Lifecycle commands (run as `ndmoadmin`)

```bash
cd /var/www/disaster-project-mis

# View state
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml ps
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml logs --tail=200 -f web

# Start / stop / restart
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml up -d
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml down        # Stops; volumes persist
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml restart web

# Apply code / image updates
git pull
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml build web
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml up -d web   # Recreate with new image

# One-off Django commands
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec web ./manage.py migrate
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec web ./manage.py createsuperuser
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec web ./manage.py shell
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec web ./manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# PostgreSQL
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec postgres psql -U postgres -d vbos

# Rebuild frontend and redeploy
cd vbos-frontend && pnpm install && pnpm build && cd ..
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml restart nginx
```

::: {.callout-tip}
The canonical deploy script is `deploy/vm/deploy.sh`; prefer it over ad-hoc commands during
a real deployment.
:::

## 8.5 Django superuser management

The DRMIS Django admin site lives at `http://<host>/admin/` and is the only way to manage
application-level users, groups, and permissions. Every command below is run **from the host**
as `ndmoadmin` and is proxied into the `vm-web-1` container. The current superuser inventory is
recorded in §14.7 (pre-handover credentials).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
All commands assume `cd /var/www/disaster-project-mis` beforehand. The compose file path
(`-f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml`) is included on every `docker compose` call so the commands
work from any working directory.
:::

### 8.5.1 List all users and flag superusers

```bash
# Full inventory — one row per Django user, ordered by username:
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec web ./manage.py shell -c "
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
U = get_user_model()
for u in U.objects.all().order_by('username'):
    print(f'{u.username:20}  {u.email:35}  staff={u.is_staff}  super={u.is_superuser}  active={u.is_active}  last_login={u.last_login}')
"

# Superusers only:
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec web ./manage.py shell -c "
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
U = get_user_model()
for u in U.objects.filter(is_superuser=True):
    print(u.username, u.email, u.is_active)
"
```

### 8.5.2 Create a new superuser (interactive — recommended)

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec web ./manage.py createsuperuser
# Django will prompt for:
#   Username: <e.g. ndmo.jdoe>
#   Email:    <e.g. jdoe@ndmo.gov.vu>
#   Password: <typed twice, not echoed>
```

### 8.5.3 Create a new superuser non-interactively (scripted / bootstrap)

Use only for first-time provisioning or scripted rotation. The `DJANGO_SUPERUSER_*` env vars
are the official Django-sanctioned way and avoid leaking passwords into shell history.

```bash
DJANGO_SUPERUSER_USERNAME=ndmo.admin \
DJANGO_SUPERUSER_EMAIL=admin@ndmo.gov.vu \
DJANGO_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD='<STRONG-RANDOM-PASSWORD>' \
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec -T \
  -e DJANGO_SUPERUSER_USERNAME \
  -e DJANGO_SUPERUSER_EMAIL \
  -e DJANGO_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD \
  web ./manage.py createsuperuser --noinput
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Clear the password from the shell history (`history -d <n>` or `unset HISTFILE` before the
command) and the vault afterwards. Prefer §8.5.2 unless automation strictly requires §8.5.3.
:::

### 8.5.4 Reset an existing user's password

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec web ./manage.py changepassword admin
# Prompts twice for the new password; no need to know the old one.
```

Scripted / non-interactive reset (for bulk rotation scripts):

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec -T web ./manage.py shell -c "
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
U = get_user_model()
u = U.objects.get(username='admin')
u.set_password('<NEW-STRONG-PASSWORD>')
u.save()
print('password updated for', u.username)
"
```

### 8.5.5 Promote an existing regular user to superuser

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec -T web ./manage.py shell -c "
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
U = get_user_model()
u = U.objects.get(username='jdoe')
u.is_staff = True
u.is_superuser = True
u.save()
print(u.username, 'is now superuser')
"
```

### 8.5.6 Demote / deactivate a superuser (preferred over deletion)

Deactivation preserves the foreign-key history of what that user created or edited. Use this at
handover to retire `admin` *after* NDMO superusers are proven working.

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec -T web ./manage.py shell -c "
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
U = get_user_model()
u = U.objects.get(username='admin')
u.is_active = False        # Cannot log in
u.is_staff = False         # Cannot open /admin/
u.is_superuser = False     # No blanket permissions
u.set_unusable_password()  # Password hash blanked
u.save()
print(u.username, 'deactivated; active/staff/super =', u.is_active, u.is_staff, u.is_superuser)
"
```

### 8.5.7 Delete a user (only if you're sure)

Deletion will fail if the user owns records with `on_delete=PROTECT`; prefer §8.5.6.

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec -T web ./manage.py shell -c "
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
U = get_user_model()
U.objects.filter(username='old.username').delete()
print('deleted')
"
```

### 8.5.8 Verify superuser credentials from the command line

Useful after a rotation, before announcing the new password to operators:

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec -T web ./manage.py shell -c "
from django.contrib.auth import authenticate
u = authenticate(username='admin', password='<PASSWORD-TO-TEST>')
print('OK' if u else 'FAIL')
"
```

A `200 OK` check from the browser side (login + land on `/admin/`) is still the authoritative
proof — see the §14.8 smoke tests.

```{=html}
<div class="screenshot-slot"><div class="screenshot-slot-inner"><strong>Figure 8.5.1 — Django admin dashboard (authenticated)</strong><code>docs/screenshots/host/29-django-admin-dashboard.png</code><span class="hint">Log into <code>http://10.4.26.55/admin/</code> as the current superuser and capture the landing page showing the list of installed apps (Users, Groups, Disasters, Rasters, etc.). This proves the superuser credential works end-to-end.</span><span class="annotate"><strong>Redact:</strong> mask the username in the top-right corner before publishing if the screenshot leaves the NDMO vault.</span></div></div>
```

# 9. Routine operations & runbooks

## 9.1 Daily health check (≤ 2 min)

```bash
uptime
df -h /
free -h
docker compose -f /var/www/disaster-project-mis/deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml ps
curl -sSf -o /dev/null -w "SPA   : %{http_code}\n"  http://10.4.26.55/
curl -sSf -o /dev/null -w "API   : %{http_code}\n"  http://10.4.26.55/api/
curl -sSf -o /dev/null -w "Admin : %{http_code}\n"  http://10.4.26.55/admin/
curl -sSf -o /dev/null -w "Tiles : %{http_code}\n"  http://10.4.26.55/titiler/
```

All four should return `200` or `302`. Investigate anything else.

```{=html}
<div class="screenshot-slot"><div class="screenshot-slot-inner"><strong>Figure 9.1.1 — Daily health check output</strong><code>docs/screenshots/host/30-daily-health.png</code><span class="hint">Capture one terminal showing the full §9.1 sequence run end-to-end, with the four <code>SPA / API / Admin / Tiles</code> lines all returning 200 or 302.</span></div></div>
```

## 9.2 Runbook — site returns 502 Bad Gateway

1. `docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml ps` — is `vm-web-1` up?
2. If not: `docker compose -f … logs --tail=200 web`. Common causes:
   - DB not ready → wait or `docker compose … logs postgres`
   - Migration error → `docker compose … exec web ./manage.py migrate`
   - Missing env var → check `vbos-backend/.env`
3. If `vm-web-1` is up: check it from nginx — `docker compose … exec nginx wget -qO- http://web:8000/api/`
4. Check nginx logs — `docker compose … logs --tail=200 nginx`

## 9.3 Runbook — disk full on `/`

```bash
df -h /
du -sh /var/lib/docker/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail
docker system df
docker image prune -a             # Remove dangling images (safe)
docker builder prune              # Remove build cache
journalctl --vacuum-time=14d
```

If still tight, extend the LV (§5.3).

## 9.4 Runbook — database grew unexpectedly

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec postgres \
    psql -U postgres -d vbos -c "\l+"
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec postgres \
    psql -U postgres -d vbos -c "\dt+"
# Per-table size:
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec postgres \
    psql -U postgres -d vbos -c \
    "SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) AS size \
     FROM pg_catalog.pg_statio_user_tables ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC LIMIT 20;"
```

## 9.5 Planned reboot procedure

```bash
# 1. Pre-reboot: snapshot state
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml ps > ~/reboot-snapshot-$(date +%F).txt
uptime >> ~/reboot-snapshot-$(date +%F).txt

# 2. Take a DB backup (see §10)
# 3. Shut down the stack cleanly
cd /var/www/disaster-project-mis
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml down

# 4. Reboot
sudo reboot

# 5. After boot, verify stack auto-starts (compose has `restart: always`)
sleep 60 && docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml ps
```

# 10. Backups & disaster recovery

## 10.1 Current state

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| Database backups | **Not scheduled** — `vbos-backend/backups/` is empty except for stub code |
| Media backups | **Not scheduled** |
| Configuration backups | In Git (this repo) |
| Offsite copy | **None** |
| Restore drill | **Never performed on this host** |

::: {.callout-important}
**This is a critical gap.** See §13. What follows is the recommended scheme to adopt.
:::

## 10.2 Recommended database backup (daily)

Save to `/mnt/ndmo_share/backups/drmis/` (on the 10 TiB PERC volume), then copy offsite.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /usr/local/bin/drmis-db-backup.sh
set -euo pipefail
DEST=/mnt/ndmo_share/backups/drmis
STAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
mkdir -p "$DEST"
docker compose -f /var/www/disaster-project-mis/deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml \
  exec -T postgres pg_dump -U postgres -Fc -d vbos \
  > "$DEST/vbos-$STAMP.dump"
find "$DEST" -name 'vbos-*.dump' -mtime +30 -delete
```

Schedule via `cron` as `ndmoadmin`:

```
15 2 * * *  /usr/local/bin/drmis-db-backup.sh >> /var/log/drmis-db-backup.log 2>&1
```

## 10.3 Recommended media backup (daily)

```bash
rsync -a --delete /var/www/disaster-project-mis/vbos-backend/media/ \
                  /mnt/ndmo_share/backups/drmis/media/
```

## 10.4 Restore procedure

```bash
# 1. Stop web so no writes happen
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml stop web celery-worker celery-beat

# 2. Drop & recreate DB
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec postgres \
  psql -U postgres -c "DROP DATABASE vbos;"
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec postgres \
  psql -U postgres -c "CREATE DATABASE vbos OWNER postgres;"

# 3. Restore
cat /mnt/ndmo_share/backups/drmis/vbos-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.dump | \
  docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml exec -T postgres \
  pg_restore -U postgres -d vbos

# 4. Restore media
rsync -a /mnt/ndmo_share/backups/drmis/media/ \
         /var/www/disaster-project-mis/vbos-backend/media/

# 5. Restart stack and verify
docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml up -d
```

## 10.5 Bare-metal rebuild outline (loss of host)

1. Arrange new hardware or reuse the same R750 after a storage failure.
2. Reinstall Ubuntu 24.04 via iDRAC Virtual Media + ISO.
3. Recreate `ndmoadmin` account, deploy SSH keys, harden SSH (§4.4).
4. Install Docker Engine (per `docs/DEPLOYMENT_VM.md §1`).
5. `git clone` this repository to `/var/www/disaster-project-mis`.
6. Restore `vbos-backend/.env` from password vault.
7. Restore frontend env files, run `pnpm install && pnpm build`.
8. Restore `media/` and the DB dump (§10.4).
9. `docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml up -d`.
10. Smoke-test against §9.1.

# 11. Monitoring & logging

## 11.1 Logs

| Source | Location / command |
|---|---|
| Linux journal | `journalctl -xe`, `journalctl -u docker`, `journalctl -u ssh` |
| `/var/log/` | `auth.log`, `syslog`, `fail2ban.log`, `samba/log.*` |
| Nginx access / error | `docker compose -f deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml logs nginx` |
| Django | `docker compose -f … logs web` |
| TiTiler | `docker compose -f … logs titiler` |
| PostgreSQL | `docker compose -f … logs postgres` |
| Hardware SEL | iDRAC UI → Maintenance → System Event Log, or `racadm getsel` |
| Lifecycle Log | iDRAC UI → Maintenance → Lifecycle Log |

## 11.2 Rotation

- `logrotate` ships default rules under `/etc/logrotate.d/`.
- Docker container logs use the default JSON driver — consider setting
  `log-opts: {max-size: "50m", max-file: "5"}` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and restarting Docker.

## 11.3 Metrics & alerting

Not currently installed. Recommended to add at minimum:

- `node_exporter` + Prometheus scrape (ministry Prometheus if available), or
- Grafana Cloud / Datadog agent for push-based monitoring, or
- iDRAC email alerts (already possible — just needs SMTP configured, see §3.4).

# 12. Security

## 12.1 Control matrix (current)

| Layer | Control | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Physical | Data-centre access | Ministry-managed (out of scope) |
| OOB | iDRAC credentials | VBoS holds `root` (recorded in §14.7); must be disabled and replaced with per-operator NDMO accounts at handover |
| Network | Host firewall (UFW) | **Active** (default deny-in, allow-out) — but Cockpit (9090), SMB (139/445) and 443 are open to `Anywhere` (§6.3) |
| Network | fail2ban on SSH | **Active** — 1 jail (`sshd`), 0 currently banned, 0 total banned to date |
| OS | SSH hardening (no root, no password, allow-list) | Active (`AllowUsers ndmoadmin`) |
| OS | Unattended security upgrades | Active |
| OS | TLS (application) | **Missing** — HTTP only on :80 |
| OS | TLS (Cockpit) | **Self-signed** — should be replaced with a CA-signed cert in `/etc/cockpit/ws-certs.d/` |
| Management | Cockpit exposure | **Open to Anywhere on 9090/tcp** — must be restricted to admin VLAN / VPN |
| Management | cloud-init network ownership | Enabled — will rewrite netplan at every boot (§14.4 Step B disables it) |
| App | Django `DEBUG=false` | Active |
| App | Django `SECRET_KEY` rotation | Unknown — rotate at handover (§14.7) |
| App | DB default credentials | **Not rotated** — `postgres/postgres` |
| App | 2FA for Django admin | Implemented but not enforced org-wide |
| Services | Samba `guest ok = yes` on 10 TiB share | **Risk — see §7.2** |
| Services | NFS daemons running with no exports | **Risk — see §7.3** |
| Services | Desktop services (`ModemManager`, `wpa_supplicant`) running | Remove |

## 12.2 Priority remediations

1. Rotate iDRAC `root` password; create per-operator iDRAC accounts.
2. **Tighten UFW: 9090/tcp (Cockpit) to admin VLAN / VPN only, 139+445 (SMB) to share-client subnet only, 443/tcp stays open for the future TLS listener.**
3. Add TLS (Let's Encrypt via a nginx `http-01` challenge, or a ministry-issued certificate) and redirect all `:80` to `:443`.
4. Install a CA-signed TLS cert for Cockpit at `/etc/cockpit/ws-certs.d/` (see §7.4).
5. Rotate the PostgreSQL password and bake it into `.env`; do **not** hard-code `postgres/postgres` any more.
6. Restrict the Samba share to authenticated users or disable it.
7. Disable NFS daemons or block 111/2049 in UFW.
8. Remove `ModemManager` and `wpa_supplicant`.
9. Close `8000/tcp` and `8002/tcp` on the host firewall — they are reachable through nginx and don't need direct exposure. Note: Docker's iptables rules bypass UFW; bind the publish to `127.0.0.1` in `deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml` instead.
10. Stand up scheduled backups (§10).

---

# 13. Known gaps & production-readiness checklist

This section tracks every item that prevents the host from being called "production-grade".
Each item is actionable.

- [ ] **TLS.** No HTTPS. Install a CA-signed certificate on nginx (or a Let's Encrypt cert if a public DNS name is available), redirect `80 → 443`, and set `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT` / HSTS in Django.
- [ ] **Database credentials.** Rotate `postgres` password away from the compose default.
- [ ] **Django `SECRET_KEY`.** Confirm it has been rotated away from `local-dev-secret-change-in-production`; if not, rotate and redeploy.
- [ ] **Redis + Celery.** Currently not deployed on the VM. Email OTP, background imports, and scheduled tasks (`celery-beat`) are therefore inoperative. Add them to `deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml`.
- [ ] **Email.** No SMTP configured; password resets and OTP cannot be delivered.
- [ ] **Backups.** No schedule, no offsite copy, no drill (§10).
- [ ] **Monitoring.** No external health check, no metrics export, no alerting.
- [ ] **iDRAC users.** Only `root` exists — create per-operator named accounts before handover (§3.4).
- [ ] **iDRAC TLS.** Replace self-signed cert with CA-signed (§3.9, §12).
- [ ] **iDRAC IPv4.** Convert from DHCP (10.4.26.51) to a formally reserved static IP (§14.5).
- [ ] **iDRAC email alerts.** SMTP not configured (§3.9).
- [ ] **Host DNS realignment — mandatory before handover.** The host resolves DNS via public `8.8.8.8 / 1.1.1.1`, but the server sits on the **Vanuatu Government (GoV) private network** (`vangov.local`) and its own iDRAC already uses the correct GoV resolvers `10.255.134.24 / 10.255.134.5`. This is a **live misconfiguration**, not a cosmetic issue: `vangov.local` names do not resolve from the host, every DNS lookup needlessly egresses the GoV WAN, and the two sides of the same machine disagree about what "DNS" means. Fix via the drop-in in §14.4 Step B before the physical move, and capture Figure 14.4.1 as evidence.
- [ ] **RAID-5 single-fault domain.** Either reshape to RAID-6 **or** assign a persistent hot spare; neither is in place today (§5).
- [ ] **DRMIS data relocation.** `vbos-backend/raster_data/` and the `vm_postgres_data` Docker volume currently live on the 100 GiB OS LV on the BOSS-S2 mirror, not on the 65.5 TiB PERC volume. Create `lv_rasters`, `lv_vectors`, `lv_postgres`, `lv_backups` on `vg_data` per the proposed layout in §2.4, migrate the data, and update the compose bind-mounts / symlinks. Without this, `/` fills the moment real COGs are ingested.
- [ ] **Timezone.** Set `Pacific/Efate` (§4.3).
- [ ] **Samba exposure.** Disable anonymous write (§7.2).
- [ ] **NFS exposure.** Disable or firewall (§7.3).
- [ ] **Desktop services.** Remove `ModemManager`, `wpa_supplicant`.
- [ ] **Cockpit exposure.** UFW currently allows 9090/tcp from `Anywhere`; restrict to admin VLAN / VPN and install a CA-signed TLS cert (§7.4, §12).
- [ ] **Docker bypass of UFW.** `8000/tcp` and `8002/tcp` are published via Docker's iptables chain (not gated by UFW); either bind to `127.0.0.1` in `deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml` or add explicit `DOCKER-USER` rules.
- [ ] **Cloud-init network ownership.** Disable `cloud-init`'s network config so netplan edits survive reboots (`/etc/cloud/cloud.cfg.d/99-disable-network-config.cfg`, §14.4).
- [ ] **DIMM population.** Only 2 of 32 DIMM slots populated — plan a memory upgrade for full multi-channel operation if the workload grows (§2.3).
- [ ] **`DJANGO_VM_HOST`.** Align with actual host IP (currently `10.252.0.158` vs real `10.4.26.55`).
- [ ] **BIOS / iDRAC / PERC firmware.** Quarterly review cadence documented and followed.
- [ ] **Change log.** Start keeping a per-server change log — ideally in this repo as `docs/CHANGELOG_HOST.md`.

# 14. Handover to NDMO

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
This chapter is the **authoritative handover runbook from VBoS (current administrator) to
NDMO**.

**Network framing (important).** The server is physically at the **VBoS office in Port
Vila** today, and will physically move to an **NDMO facility** at handover (Option 1,
confirmed). **Both sites sit on the same logical network** — the Vanuatu Government (GoV)
private WAN / `vangov.local` intranet. The "migration" is therefore **not crossing networks**;
it is a physical move plus a **subnet reassignment within the GoV WAN** (VBoS-allocated
`10.4.26.0/24` → NDMO-allocated subnet issued by NDMO networking).

Two consequences of this framing shape the whole runbook:

1. **Pre-handover dry runs are possible.** Because NDMO seats are already on the GoV WAN,
   NDMO sysadmins can SSH / open the iDRAC UI / open Cockpit **today** (subject to GoV WAN
   ACLs) against the current VBoS-segment addresses — before any cable is unplugged. §14.3
   adds a dedicated NDMO dry-run step.
2. **No DHCP detour is needed at cutover.** The clean path is to **pre-allocate** the new
   NDMO static IPs in a netplan drop-in (host) and via `racadm` (iDRAC) *while the server is
   still at VBoS*, so at boot at the NDMO rack the correct static address comes up in one
   step. The DHCP-detour route is documented in §14.4.x as a **fallback only**, to be used
   if the pre-allocation path is blocked (e.g. NDMO-side DHCP reservation can't be arranged
   in time).

Follow this chapter in order. Do not skip the credential-rotation and sign-off steps; each
one is recorded in §14.9.
:::

## 14.1 Pre-handover state

### Physical — where the server is today

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Site | **VBoS office, Port Vila, Vanuatu** |
| Rack / server room | VBoS server room (exact rack + U position to be confirmed in Appendix C) |
| Power | VBoS A/B feeds, both live — §2.6 confirms both PSU inputs energised |
| Switch port | VBoS-owned 1 GbE access port, untagged on the VBoS-segment VLAN |
| Chassis | Dell PowerEdge R750, service tag `BCLLJ54`, Express Service Code `24706476328` |

### Logical — what the server is connected to

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| WAN / intranet | **Vanuatu Government (GoV) private network**, domain `vangov.local` (**unchanged** at handover) |
| Authoritative DNS | `10.255.134.24`, `10.255.134.5` — GoV/ministry resolvers, reachable across the whole GoV WAN |
| NDMO reachability today | **Already reachable** from NDMO seats on the GoV WAN (subject to WAN ACLs) — this is what makes the §14.3 NDMO dry run possible |

### IP allocation — the piece that changes

| Item | Today (VBoS segment) | At handover (NDMO segment) |
|---|---|---|
| Host `eno8303` | `10.4.26.55/24`, gateway `10.4.26.1` | New NDMO-issued static IP + gateway (pre-allocated — §14.4 Step A) |
| iDRAC dedicated NIC | `10.4.26.51/24` via **DHCP**, MAC `d0:46:0c:63:34:4a` | New NDMO-issued static IP (pre-set via `racadm` — §14.5) |
| Netplan file | `/etc/netplan/50-cloud-init.yaml` (cloud-init-managed — see §14.4 Step B) | Same file + a new drop-in `99-ndmo-static.yaml` with the new static IP |
| Host DNS servers | `8.8.8.8`, `1.1.1.1` — **live misconfiguration, to fix at cutover** (§14.4 Step C) | `10.255.134.24`, `10.255.134.5` — matches iDRAC, matches GoV standard |

### Credentials, application, TLS

| Item | Value at time of writing |

| Host credentials | `ssh ndmoadmin@10.4.26.55` (SSH key only; password auth disabled) — held by VBoS, recorded in §14.7 |
| iDRAC credentials | `https://10.4.26.51/` — `root` held by VBoS, recorded in §14.7 |
| Cockpit credentials | `https://10.4.26.55:9090/` — logs in with the OS shell account (`ndmoadmin`) |
| Database credentials | Default `postgres / postgres` inside the compose network (§13 flags this for rotation) |
| Django secret key | In `vbos-backend/.env` — **VBoS to rotate before sign-off** (§14.7.1) |
| Domain / DNS name | None — accessed by IP only |
| TLS (application) | None — HTTP on port 80 only |
| TLS (Cockpit) | Self-signed default cert |

## 14.2 Handover phases overview

```
Phase 1  Pre-flight + snapshot (at VBoS, over GoV WAN)     §14.3 steps 1–3
Phase 2  NDMO dry-run          (NDMO seats reach server    §14.3 step 4
                                across the GoV WAN)
Phase 3  Pre-allocate NDMO     (netplan drop-in + racadm,  §14.4 step A
         static IPs             BEFORE any cable move)       §14.5 step A
Phase 4  Host DNS realignment  (8.8.8.8/1.1.1.1 →           §14.4 step C
                                10.255.134.24/5)
Phase 5  Physical move         (power-down, ship,           (logistics, not
         (VBoS → NDMO)          re-rack)                     in scope here)
Phase 6  Cutover               (power-up at NDMO rack;       §14.4 step D
                                netplan applies new static    §14.5 step B
                                in ONE step — no DHCP
                                detour needed)
         — fallback route: DHCP detour                       §14.4 step B'
Phase 7  Application config realignment                     §14.6
Phase 8  Transfer pre-handover credentials (vault)          §14.7
Phase 9  Credential rotation (all secrets)                  §14.7.1
Phase 10 Smoke tests & NDMO-side validation                 §14.8
Phase 11 Formal sign-off + credential purge                 §14.9
```

::: {.callout-note}
Phases 1–4 run entirely **before the server leaves VBoS**. Because VBoS and NDMO are on the
same GoV WAN, NDMO sysadmins can validate reachability (Phase 2) and the pre-allocated IP
configuration (Phase 3) without any cable move. Only Phase 5 requires downtime; Phase 6 is
a single netplan-apply on first boot at the NDMO rack.
:::

## 14.3 Pre-flight — before the move

Run through this list **on-site at VBoS**, over the GoV WAN, while the server is still in
the VBoS rack and reachable from both the VBoS admin workstation and the NDMO sysadmin
workstations. Steps 1–3 are executed by VBoS; step 4 is the **NDMO dry-run** and is executed
by an NDMO sysadmin from their own seat.

Once the server is powered down for the physical move (Phase 5), recovery requires
physical / crash-cart access at the NDMO rack — so everything that can be validated beforehand
should be validated beforehand.

1. **Full on-host snapshot of state.**

   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/handover-$(date +%F)
   cd ~/handover-$(date +%F)
   hostnamectl                       > 01-hostnamectl.txt
   lsb_release -a                    > 02-lsb_release.txt
   uname -a                          > 03-uname.txt
   ip -brief addr                    > 04-ip-addr.txt
   ip route                          > 05-ip-route.txt
   resolvectl status                 > 06-resolvectl.txt
   sudo ss -tlnp                     > 07-ss-tlnp.txt
   sudo ufw status verbose           > 08-ufw.txt
   sudo iptables -S                  > 08b-iptables.txt
   sudo fail2ban-client status sshd  > 08c-fail2ban.txt
   systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager > 09-services.txt
   lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,SERIAL,ROTA,TRAN > 10-lsblk.txt
   sudo pvs && sudo vgs && sudo lvs  > 11-lvm.txt 2>&1
   docker compose -f /var/www/disaster-project-mis/deploy/vm/docker-compose.yml ps > 12-docker-ps.txt
   docker images                     > 13-docker-images.txt
   docker volume ls                  > 14-docker-volumes.txt
   sudo cat /etc/netplan/50-cloud-init.yaml > 15-netplan-before.txt
   sudo dmidecode -s system-serial-number > 15a-service-tag.txt
   sudo dmidecode -t 17              > 15b-dimm-inventory.txt
   sudo dmidecode -t 39              > 15c-psu-inventory.txt
   racadm getsysinfo                 > 16-idrac-sysinfo.txt 2>&1 || true
   racadm get iDRAC.IPv4             > 16a-idrac-ipv4.txt 2>&1 || true
   racadm get iDRAC.Users            > 16b-idrac-users.txt 2>&1 || true
   ```

2. **Database & media backup** to the 10 TiB share *and* to an external drive:

   ```bash
   sudo /usr/local/bin/drmis-db-backup.sh     # From §10.2 (create it first if absent)
   rsync -a /var/www/disaster-project-mis/vbos-backend/media/ \
            /mnt/ndmo_share/backups/drmis/media/
   ```

   Copy `/mnt/ndmo_share/backups/drmis/` onto an external USB disk and take it to NDMO as a
   physical Plan-B in case the network-configured restore fails.

3. **Export iDRAC config** for later diffing:

   ```bash
   # Using the racadm wrapper (§3.8), from the host:
   racadm get -f ~/handover-$(date +%F)/17-idrac-export.xml -t xml
   # Plus a full Server Configuration Profile export (used by Dell support):
   # iDRAC UI → Configuration → Server Configuration Profile → Export
   # Or via racadm:
   racadm systemconfig export -f ~/handover-$(date +%F)/17b-scp.xml -t xml -l local
   ```

4. **NDMO dry-run over the GoV WAN.** Because VBoS and NDMO are on the same GoV network
   (`vangov.local`), NDMO sysadmins can validate reachability and credentials **before any
   cable is unplugged**. Do this at least 48 hours before the physical move, so any GoV WAN
   ACL or NDMO firewall rule that needs to be opened has time to clear change control.

   **Executed by an NDMO sysadmin from an NDMO seat** (not from the VBoS office):

   ```bash
   # a. Basic reachability across the GoV WAN
   ping -c3 10.4.26.55         # host (DMIS)
   ping -c3 10.4.26.51         # iDRAC

   # b. SSH to the host with VBoS-issued credentials (Option B handover package, §14.7)
   ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new ndmoadmin@10.4.26.55 "hostnamectl && uptime"
   # Expected: Ubuntu 24.04.x, ndmo-drmis-01, uptime > 0

   # c. iDRAC web UI
   #    Open https://10.4.26.51/ in a browser on the NDMO seat.
   #    Log in as root with the §14.7 password.
   #    Confirm: the dashboard loads, service tag = BCLLJ54, firmware = 7.10.50.00.

   # d. Cockpit
   #    Open https://10.4.26.55:9090/ ; accept the self-signed cert; log in as ndmoadmin.

   # e. Application endpoints (optional but confirms the full stack is reachable)
   curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "SPA %{http_code}\n"  http://10.4.26.55/
   curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "API %{http_code}\n"  http://10.4.26.55/api/
   curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "Adm %{http_code}\n"  http://10.4.26.55/admin/
   ```

   **Success criteria** (all must pass before Phase 5 is scheduled):

   - a, b, c, d all succeed from the NDMO seat;
   - e returns 200 / 301 / 302 (not connection refused, not timeout);
   - the NDMO sysadmin has written down the iDRAC service tag / firmware from the UI and
     compared it against §14.1 — proves they reached the right box, not a lookalike.

   **If any of a–d fails**, raise a GoV WAN ticket immediately — the fix is a networking
   issue on the GoV backbone or the NDMO edge, not on the server, and must be resolved
   before the physical move otherwise cutover can't be validated remotely either.


5. **Freeze the application repo.** On a development workstation:
   - `git status` clean, everything pushed;
   - Tag the current commit, e.g. `git tag -a handover-$(date +%F) -m "NDMO handover baseline" && git push --tags`.

6. **Document current credentials** (once, in the ministry password vault):
   - `ndmoadmin` password (even though SSH is key-only, `sudo` needs it — set one and record it);
   - All SSH public keys currently in `~ndmoadmin/.ssh/authorized_keys`;
   - iDRAC named admin password;
   - Database password (if rotated away from `postgres`);
   - Django `SECRET_KEY` (not the whole `.env`, just that value);
   - AWS / S3 keys if `DJANGO_AWS_*` are populated in `.env`.
